title: Start with weakness
hookLine: philosophy begins with noticing your own weakness (Discourses 2.11)

cards: Nobody walks into a calculus class insisting they already know calculus. Nobody sits down at a piano for the first time convinced they can play Chopin. With those things, we know what we don't know.
But ask a room full of people what's fair, what a good life is, or how to treat a difficult relative, and plenty of people are sure they already know.
Epictetus found that strange, and said it's exactly where philosophy has to begin.

teach.b: This is Discourses book two, chapter eleven: what the beginning of philosophy is.
For anyone who comes in by the right door, Epictetus says, it begins with noticing your own weakness and inability in the things that matter most. Why there?

teach.h: NO ONE IS BORN KNOWING GEOMETRY.
teach.b: Nobody is born with an idea of a right triangle, or of a musical interval.

teach.h: WE ALL THINK WE KNOW WHAT'S GOOD.
teach.b: We learn those from teachers, so nobody who hasn't learned them thinks they know them. But good and bad, fair and unfair, noble and shameful: everyone arrives with some sense of those.

We're born with the outline, and because we have it, we assume we know how to fill it in. That's the trap. Two people can both love justice and still disagree completely about what's just in a given case.
You can't both be right, and seeming right to yourself isn't enough; people who are wrong feel just as certain.

So philosophy starts by admitting that, and then looks for a standard, the way people found the balance for weighing and the rule for measuring straight lines, so that arguments could be settled by something outside our feelings.
Weakness here doesn't mean you're bad. It means you're honest about being unfinished.
The person who says, I don't actually know how to handle my anger, is further along than the person who's sure they've got it figured out.

how: Some people who practice Stoicism begin by naming an area where they feel certain but may be wrong, and treat that honest admission as the start of their training.

o: laziness that keeps a student from studying
weakness: seeing you're less sure than you think
the shame of losing an argument in public

games.q: start with weakness: tap the pairs.
p: we know we have to learn them

s: Epictetus says philosophy begins with confidence in what you know
it begins with noticing your own weakness in the things that matter most.
he says we're born with a rough sense of good and bad
and that's why we wrongly assume we know how to apply it.
for Epictetus, feeling certain proves you're right
people who are wrong feel just as certain, so we need a standard.

games.q: two of your students both love justice, and they disagree completely about a case. you're Epictetus. what do you say?
o: each is right in his own way.
you can't both be right; we need a standard outside your feelings.
games.why: he says seeming right isn't enough, and philosophy looks for a standard, the way people found the balance and the rule.

practice: Ask yourself, gently: where am I sure I'm right, and might not be? Let one come up, about a person, a decision, a way of doing things, and say plainly inside: here, I'm not as strong as I think.
Notice whether that feels uncomfortable or like a strange relief, and let the admission be a beginning.

wordCard.voice: Astheneia. Greek for weakness: Epictetus' door into philosophy, noticing that in the things that matter most, we're less sure and less able than we think.

orig.note: Greek astheneia: weakness, lack of strength; Epictetus says philosophy begins with awareness of it.

carryVoice: Your line: honest about being unfinished. That's the right door into philosophy. See you tomorrow.
